# CI performance investigation: pull request #20124

## Executive summary

PR [#20124](https://github.com/open-telemetry/opentelemetry-java-instrumentation/pull/20124)
is small in repository-impact terms: at head
`98b67c1f9591dc3b0dcbd82cdc8bc900ddea473c` it changes seven Java files in five
leaf Javaagent projects across four instrumentation families (Dubbo, JAX-RS,
MongoDB, and Redisson), plus one reflection-guidance document. It changes no
shared production module, Gradle build file, dependency catalog, or workflow.

Nevertheless, its first build attempt at that SHA ran the repository's standard
PR suite almost in full:

* 90 jobs were represented: 85 successful, two substantive failures, one failed
  aggregate status job, and two intentionally skipped jobs.
* The attempt took about 71 minutes wall clock, from workflow creation at
  21:23:06 UTC until the retry began at 22:34 UTC.
* Completed jobs consumed about **3,226 runner-minutes (53.8 runner-hours)**.
* The dominant cost was 56 all-repository test jobs: **2,710 runner-minutes**,
  a 48.7-minute median, and a 65.8-minute maximum.
* Four latest-dependency jobs added 237 runner-minutes, nine smoke-test jobs
  149, and four Muzzle jobs 58.
* CodeQL was a separate 32-minute workflow, of which 27m12s was its deliberately
  uncached whole-repository `assemble`.

The main explanation is not a Gradle incrementality failure in the changed
modules. The workflow does not use changed modules to select ordinary tests,
latest-dependency tests, Muzzle, smoke tests, assembly, formatting, or CodeQL.
Its only path-based decisions are whether to run native tests and whether to
build servlet images. Everything else is intentionally repository-wide.

Incrementality also has little opportunity to help. Every matrix cell starts in
a fresh checkout, so ordinary Gradle up-to-date state is absent. Cross-job reuse
must come from the build cache. In representative PR jobs, it did not:

* `common / build`: 5,355 actionable tasks, **5,355 executed**, zero reported
  from cache; Gradle took 33m39s.
* `common / test2 (25, hotspot, indy true)`: 2,416 actionable tasks, 2,384
  executed and 32 up-to-date; Gradle took 56m39s.
* `testLatestDeps0`: 1,801 actionable tasks, 1,769 executed and 32 up-to-date;
  Gradle took 54m43s.
* Muzzle did somewhat better, but only 135 of 2,024 tasks came from cache.

There is evidence of a cache-access regression around the September 1
Develocity migration. A main-branch `common / build` immediately preceding this
PR used the community Develocity instance and got 1,504 of 5,355 tasks from
cache, finishing its Gradle work in 23m42s. The PR job published its scan to the
anonymous `gradle.com` service and got zero task-cache hits, despite starting
after that main build had completed. Before the migration, a comparable PR build
on August 31 got 312 cache hits and took 30m57s. This does not explain the
majority of the roughly one-hour critical path—the full test matrix does—but it
is a concrete avoidable loss and merits immediate verification.

The strongest opportunities are therefore:

1. restore effective read access to the community remote build cache for PRs;
2. make PR test/Muzzle/latest-dependency selection module-aware, with the full
   matrix on main, merge queue, nightly runs, or an explicit label;
3. stop repeating whole-repository discovery and multi-gigabyte cache setup in
   every matrix cell;
4. retain the inexpensive global checks and the intentionally broad security
   checks unless policy changes.

## Scope of the PR

The GitHub PR API reports 8 files, 128 additions, and 37 deletions:

| Area | Changed project/file |
| --- | --- |
| Dubbo | `instrumentation/apache-dubbo-2.7/javaagent` |
| JAX-RS 2 | `instrumentation/jaxrs/jaxrs-2.0/jaxrs-2.0-annotations/javaagent` |
| JAX-RS 3 | `instrumentation/jaxrs/jaxrs-3.0/jaxrs-3.0-annotations/javaagent` |
| MongoDB | `instrumentation/mongo/mongo-4.0/javaagent` |
| Redisson | `instrumentation/redisson/redisson-metrics-2.3/javaagent` (three files) |
| Documentation | `.github/agents/knowledge/java-reflection.md` |

The Java edits cache reflective lookups. There is no change to core agent
tooling, shared testing infrastructure, dependency management, Gradle plugins,
or CI configuration. In a module-aware system this would naturally select five
leaf projects, their directly affected compatibility tests, and a small set of
cross-cutting safety checks.

## What the workflows actually select

### Path detection is limited to two optional job families

`.github/workflows/build-pull-request.yml` has no top-level `paths` filter. Its
two resolver jobs inspect PR files only to:

* enable native tests for native-relevant library, smoke-test, or top-level
  build changes (`build-pull-request.yml:36-68`); and
* enable servlet image builds for servlet image or workflow changes
  (`build-pull-request.yml:70-93`).

For this PR both resolved false, so `test-native` and `build-servlet-images`
were skipped. That is the only meaningful saving obtained from the small diff.
The dispatcher then calls `reusable-pr-build.yml`, which always invokes:

* `common`;
* `test-latest-deps`;
* four Muzzle partitions;
* lint; and
* the final aggregate status check.

### The common test matrix is repository-wide

`build-common.yml:277-305` defines:

* seven Java modes: 8, 11, 17, 21, 25, 25 with unsafe denied, and 26;
* four test partitions; and
* indy false and true.

OpenJ9 is skipped by default for PRs, but the remaining Cartesian product is
**7 × 4 × 2 = 56 jobs**.

Each job first runs:

```text
./gradlew check -x spotlessCheck listTestsInPartition -PtestPartition=N
```

The root build logic in `build.gradle.kts:89-129` configures every subproject,
collects every `Test` task, and assigns projects round-robin modulo four. It
does not inspect the PR diff or the Gradle dependency graph. The second Gradle
invocation runs every test task listed for that repository-wide partition under
the selected Java/indy mode.

That explains why this PR tested Quarkus, Lettuce, Tomcat, Vert.x, and hundreds
of other unrelated modules. It also explains the unrelated failures:

* `test0 (17, hotspot, indy false)` failed after 6m28s of its Gradle test phase
  because the unrelated Quarkus 3.9 project could not resolve
  `io.quarkus:quarkus-rest-kotlin:3.9.1`.
* `test1 (17, hotspot, indy true)` failed after 41 minutes because the unrelated
  Lettuce 5.0 `testStableSemconv` task exceeded its 15-minute timeout.

The matrix has `fail-fast: false`, so these failures did not stop other cells.
The required status check also waits on all reusable-workflow groups. That is
appropriate for collecting complete failure information, but it means an
unrelated failure discovered at 11.8 job-minutes still leaves the PR waiting
for the 65–68 minute critical-path jobs. GitHub's failed-job retry subsequently
reran the failed jobs rather than requiring a new commit, but the first attempt
had already spent 53.8 runner-hours.

### Other broad work

* `reusable-test-latest-deps.yml:20-86` runs the same four repository-wide
  partitions with `-PtestLatestDeps=true`; there is no changed-module filter.
* `reusable-muzzle.yml:14-45` always runs all four repository-wide Muzzle
  partitions.
* `build-common.yml:403-477` runs all nine Ubuntu smoke suites in reduced
  app-server mode. “Reduced” reduces cases inside suites; it does not select
  suites from changed paths.
* `build-common.yml:211-275` runs root `check`, `javadoc`, `sourcesJar`, and
  `spdxSbom` with tests skipped. On this repository that still scheduled 5,355
  tasks.
* `build-common.yml:29-209` separately runs Spotless, license generation, FOSSA
  generation, and several repository-wide scripts.
* `codeql.yml:77-85` deliberately runs whole-repository
  `assemble -x javadoc --no-build-cache --no-daemon`; the comments correctly
  state that disabling the build cache is required so CodeQL observes every
  compilation.

## Timing and fan-out

All times below are from GitHub's job and step timestamps for build run
[34719797570](https://github.com/open-telemetry/opentelemetry-java-instrumentation/actions/runs/34719797570),
attempt 1, unless noted otherwise.

| Job family | Jobs | Runner-minutes | Median job | Longest job |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Common tests | 56 | 2,709.8 | 48.7m | 65.8m |
| Latest dependencies | 4 | 237.3 | 59.6m | 68.3m |
| Ubuntu smoke tests | 9 | 148.6 | 15.7m | 24.0m |
| Muzzle | 4 | 57.5 | 13.9m | 17.0m |
| Build, validation, resolvers, aggregate | 17 | 72.3 | — | 35.1m |
| **Total** | **90** | **3,225.6** | — | **68.3m** |

Within the 56 common test jobs:

| Step | Median per job | Aggregate runner-minutes |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| Test | 44.1m | 2,436.6 |
| List tests | 2.27m | 124.0 |
| Free disk space | 1.40m | 77.2 |
| Setup Gradle | 0.88m | 46.7 |
| Node setup and pnpm cache | about 0.07m combined | 3.6 |

The fan-out reduced wall time by running almost everything concurrently, but it
did not reduce work. The test matrix alone used about 45.2 runner-hours. It
also multiplied dependency/cache downloads and repository configuration 56
times.

### Queue and dispatch overhead

Queueing was not the main cause on the first attempt:

* workflow created: 21:23:06;
* resolver jobs started: approximately 21:24:20–21:24:22;
* matrix jobs started: approximately 21:24:29–21:24:30;
* within the matrix, the average recorded created-to-start delay was only about
  0.1 minute and the maximum about 0.7 minute.

CodeQL's Java job similarly began about 61 seconds after workflow creation.
Thus roughly one minute was dispatch/queue overhead; the remaining hour was
execution.

There was substantial concurrent repository traffic. A main build beginning at
20:56 ran 140 jobs, including OpenJ9, while this PR launched 89 build jobs at
21:24. Both showed long test cells. This may contribute to shared network,
container-registry, or service contention, but the available timestamps do not
prove runner CPU contention: jobs obtained runners quickly.

## Gradle incrementality and cache behavior

### Why normal incrementality does not help

Every GitHub matrix cell uses a new hosted runner and fresh checkout. Gradle's
local file snapshots and task outputs therefore do not exist at job start.
Within a single job, incrementality works: the second smoke-test invocation in
one representative job reported 1 executed and 1,608 up-to-date tasks after the
preceding build invocation. That state cannot benefit another job.

Cross-job and cross-commit incrementality therefore depends on:

1. Gradle User Home restored by `gradle/actions/setup-gradle`; and
2. the Develocity remote build cache configured in `settings.gradle.kts`.

### Dependency caches are warm but large

A representative PR job restored:

* a 195 MB Gradle User Home partial match;
* a 3,853 MB dependency cache in about 44 seconds;
* a 189 MB transform cache in about 7 seconds; and
* smaller wrapper, generated-JAR, Kotlin DSL, and Groovy DSL caches.

The exact dependency cache was useful for avoiding downloads from Maven
Central, but it is not compiled/test output reuse. Repeating a roughly 4 GB
restore across dozens of jobs is itself material network and runner overhead.
`cache-read-only: true` is appropriate for untrusted PR jobs and prevents cache
poisoning, but it also means PR results never improve subsequent PR jobs.

### Task-output cache effectiveness was near zero

Representative Gradle summaries:

| Job | Gradle duration | Actionable tasks |
| --- | ---: | --- |
| PR `common / build` | 33m39s | 5,355 executed; 0 from cache |
| PR common test2, Java 25, indy | 56m39s | 2,384 executed; 32 up-to-date |
| PR `testLatestDeps0` | 54m43s | 1,769 executed; 32 up-to-date |
| PR Muzzle partition 4 | 11m54s | 1,889 executed; 135 from cache |
| Immediately preceding main `common / build` | 23m42s | 3,851 executed; 1,504 from cache |

The main build's scan was published to
`community.develocity.cloud`; PR scans were published to the unauthenticated
`gradle.com` service. The PR workflow does not receive
`DEVELOCITY_ACCESS_KEY`, while `.github/workflows/build.yml:14-26` explicitly
passes that secret to the main `common` and latest-dependency workflows.

This distinction became more important after PR
[#19927](https://github.com/open-telemetry/opentelemetry-java-instrumentation/pull/19927)
moved the remote cache from the dedicated OpenTelemetry host to
`community.develocity.cloud` on September 1. That PR explicitly warned that the
new shared instance may require an access key for endpoints that were formerly
anonymous. PR
[#19533](https://github.com/open-telemetry/opentelemetry-java-instrumentation/pull/19533)
had verified anonymous cache reads against the *old* dedicated instance, not
the new community instance.

The evidence is consistent with PR jobs no longer reading the useful community
remote cache:

* main, with credentials, obtained 1,504 hits;
* this PR, beginning just after that main build completed and populated the
  cache, obtained zero;
* an August 31 PR, before the migration, obtained 312 hits in the comparable
  build; and
* the current PR's few Muzzle hits can be explained by the restored local cache
  snapshot rather than proving community-cache access.

This should be confirmed with Develocity cache access logs or a controlled
read-only probe, because Gradle's normal console output does not identify every
miss source. It is nevertheless the clearest concrete cache regression in the
observed data.

### Configuration cache does not rescue the test jobs

The repository enables both build and configuration caches in
`gradle.properties`. The representative common and latest-dependency tests
discarded their configuration-cache entries because Quarkus's `buildModel`
task produced 26 problems (three unique categories). These jobs also run test
discovery and tests as separate Gradle invocations with different requested
tasks/properties, reducing the chance that one configuration entry can serve
both.

The build and Muzzle jobs successfully stored configuration-cache entries, but
there is only one principal Gradle invocation in those jobs, and PR cache
snapshots are read-only. Storing the entry at job end does not speed the job
that just completed.

## Fixed cost versus avoidable cost

### Expected fixed-cost validation

These checks are broad by design or inexpensive enough not to drive wall time:

* Gradle wrapper validation: about 14 seconds.
* Zizmor: about 25 seconds.
* Dependency review: about 30 seconds.
* Modified-file lint: about 19 seconds.
* Repository scripts such as package-name and suppression-key checks: generally
  6–10 seconds each.
* Spotless: 5.1 minutes; license report: 3.4 minutes; FOSSA generation:
  3.0 minutes; Gradle plugins: 3.2 minutes. These are global, but they finish
  far before the critical path.
* CodeQL Java: 31m40s job time after a roughly one-minute queue. Its 27m12s
  uncached assemble is intentional so CodeQL can observe compilation, followed
  by 3m45s analysis. This is expensive but separate from the 68-minute build
  critical path and is a defensible security-validation cost.

### Avoidable or reducible work

* Running all project tests in 56 environment/partition cells for five changed
  leaf projects.
* Running all latest-dependency tests instead of the changed instrumentations'
  latest-dependency tests.
* Running all Muzzle partitions rather than changed javaagent modules plus
  dependents.
* Running all nine smoke suites for a PR that changed no smoke-test module or
  common agent runtime.
* Running a whole-repository `check` merely to discover test task names in
  every matrix cell.
* Restoring multi-gigabyte Gradle caches and freeing disk independently in every
  cell.
* Re-executing almost every cacheable task because useful remote cache entries
  are apparently unavailable to PR jobs.
* Allowing unrelated flaky/dependency failures to hold the required status open
  until the slowest matrix cell completes.

## Is CI actually “substantially slower lately”?

The evidence supports “consistently very expensive,” but not a large regression
within the limited comparison window:

* Among 46 non-outlier successful PR runs visible on September 12, median wall
  time was 75.3 minutes.
* Among 37 non-outlier successful runs visible from September 3–4, median wall
  time was 94.9 minutes.
* A comparable leaf-instrumentation PR on August 31 used 3,060 runner-minutes,
  had a 64.2-minute longest job, and a 64.5-minute full first-attempt wall time.
* PR #20124 used 3,226 runner-minutes, had a 68.3-minute longest job, and about a
  71-minute first attempt: roughly 5% more runner work, not a step-function
  slowdown.

The September 9 addition of a ninth Ubuntu `spring-aot` smoke suite accounts for
about 12 runner-minutes in this run but is not on the critical path. The current
build also has 95 more actionable tasks than the August 31 sample and lost 312
cache hits, explaining several additional minutes.

Therefore, this PR is a good demonstration of a longstanding scaling problem:
small diffs receive nearly the same validation as repository-wide changes. The
Develocity migration likely removed some cache effectiveness, but the full
matrix—not queueing and not the PR's module dependency graph—is the dominant
reason the run takes about an hour.

## Prioritized recommendations

### P0: restore observable, effective PR build-cache reads

1. Run a controlled PR probe against `community.develocity.cloud` with the
   GitHub Actions local build-output cache disabled. Compare anonymous access
   with authenticated read-only access and record hit counts.
2. Verify that the repository's community-instance access key has the correct
   host prefix and that main jobs are still pushing entries after the migration.
3. If the community project supports it, enable anonymous read access while
   retaining authenticated writes. That preserves fork safety.
4. If anonymous reads are unavailable, do **not** expose a reusable write-capable
   secret to arbitrary fork PR code. Use a genuinely read-only credential only
   for trusted same-repository PRs, or restore a main-written, PR-read-only
   GitHub cache containing build outputs with a bounded retention/size design.
5. Add a small cache-health signal to CI: report task hit ratio and alert when a
   representative PR build falls from thousands of expected hits to near zero.

Expected impact from the observed pair is approximately 10 minutes on
`common / build` (33m39s versus 23m42s), plus potentially much larger aggregate
savings in compilation/setup work across test and latest-dependency cells.

### P1: introduce impact-based PR validation

Build a conservative changed-project closure from the PR diff and Gradle
project dependencies:

* For leaf instrumentation changes, run tests for changed projects and their
  directly affected testing projects.
* Run Muzzle only for changed javaagent modules.
* Run latest-dependency tests only for changed instrumentations that define
  them.
* Gate smoke suites on smoke/shared-runtime changes, while retaining one cheap
  assembled-agent smoke check for ordinary javaagent changes.
* Treat changes to shared agent tooling, testing infrastructure, conventions,
  dependency management, settings, or workflows as global and retain the full
  suite.
* Provide a label to force the full matrix.
* Keep the full matrix on main or merge queue and in scheduled builds, so the
  optimization changes where exhaustive validation occurs rather than deleting
  it.

This is the only recommendation capable of removing most of the 45 test
runner-hours for a leaf-only PR.

### P1: reduce repeated matrix setup and discovery

1. Replace `./gradlew check ... listTestsInPartition` with a purpose-built task
   that can enumerate the selected project/test tasks without realizing the
   whole `check` graph.
2. Where practical, execute discovery and tests in one Gradle invocation or
   publish one generated matrix from a single preparatory job.
3. Measure whether four partitions per Java/indy pair remain optimal. Fewer,
   larger jobs would trade some parallelism for fewer 4 GB cache restores,
   fewer Gradle configurations, and less disk cleanup. Base the choice on wall
   time and total runner cost rather than job count alone.
4. Avoid provisioning Node/pnpm in partitions that contain no Vaadin task.

The currently repeated common-test overhead is at least 124 runner-minutes for
test discovery, 77 for disk cleanup, and 47 for Gradle setup per PR attempt.

### P2: repair configuration-cache compatibility

Fix the Quarkus `buildModel` task's configuration-cache violations, then verify
that the test command actually reuses a stored entry. This will not eliminate
test execution and is secondary to module selection and build-cache access, but
it can reduce repeated repository configuration and make cache behavior less
fragile.

### P2: separate fast feedback from exhaustive feedback

Return a required “leaf PR” result from changed-module tests, formatting,
Muzzle-for-changed-modules, and a representative JDK/indy pair. Run the
remaining JDK matrix and broad smoke/latest-dependency coverage as merge-queue
or non-blocking validation, escalating to required only for shared-impact
changes. This preserves coverage while reducing author feedback latency.

### P3: keep low-cost global checks unless measurements justify complexity

Path-gating wrapper validation, dependency review, Zizmor, small shell checks,
or lint would save seconds and add workflow complexity. Spotless, licenses, and
FOSSA together cost minutes but are not the wall-clock bottleneck. Optimize
them only after cache access and test selection.

## Bottom line

PR #20124 was not faster because repository CI currently equates “PR” with
“almost full repository validation.” Gradle only sees a fresh workspace in each
of 89 build jobs, task-output cache reuse was effectively absent, and the
workflow's test partitioner deliberately lists all projects rather than changed
projects. Queue time was about one minute; execution and fan-out were the cost.

Restoring remote cache reads is the quickest concrete fix, especially after the
community Develocity migration. The largest structural improvement is
conservative module-aware validation, backed by full validation on main,
merge-queue, scheduled, or explicitly requested runs.
